Spokesman
SPOKES-man
n. (one who speaks on behalf of another)
Hebrew dabar, to speak, in a construction meaning he shall speak for thee. The English compound is plain: the man who speaks. The word occurs once, of Aaron appointed to speak for Moses.

Biblical Definition

And he shall be thy spokesman unto the people: and he shall be, even he shall be to thee instead of a mouth, and thou shalt be to him instead of God. The arrangement is made after Moses has exhausted his objections at the burning bush, and the narrative does not present it as a triumph. The anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses, and then Aaron was given. God had already answered the objection directly — who hath made man's mouth? and, I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say — and Moses had asked again to be excused. The concession granted is real and is not a rebuke only; Aaron genuinely serves, and God uses him. But the structure deserves attention because it establishes a pattern that runs through Scripture. Moses receives the word and Aaron speaks it: thou shalt speak unto him, and put words in his mouth. God restates the relation in the same terms later — see, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet. A spokesman in the biblical sense has no message of his own. His entire authority is the message he was given, which is exactly the standing of every prophet, and of every preacher since. The office is high and the man in it is a mouth.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one who speaks for another; one deputed to speak in the name of another.

expand to see more

SPOKESMAN, n. One who speaks for another.

SPOKESMAN, n. One who is deputed to speak in the name or behalf of another person or of a body of men.

MOUTH, n. The aperture in the head of an animal by which it utters sounds; the instrument of speech.

PROPHET, n. One that foretells future events; one who speaks by divine inspiration, or by the impulse of the Holy Spirit.

DEPUTE, v.t. To appoint and send with a special commission to act in the place of another.

Key Scripture

Exodus 4:16 — "And he shall be thy spokesman unto the people: and he shall be, even he shall be to thee instead of a mouth, and thou shalt be to him instead of God."

Exodus 4:14 — "And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses, and he said, Is not Aaron the Levite thy brother? I know that he can speak well. And also, behold, he cometh forth to meet thee: and when he seeth thee, he will be glad in his heart."

Exodus 4:15 — "And thou shalt speak unto him, and put words in his mouth: and I will be with thy mouth, and with his mouth, and will teach you what ye shall do."

Exodus 7:1 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet."

Modern Corruption

Preaching is widely treated as the speaker's own contribution, with Scripture supplying material; the biblical spokesman has no message of his own and is answerable for delivering another's.

expand to see more

Where the sermon is built around the preacher's insight, experience, or personality, with texts recruited to support it, the office has been inverted. Aaron's commission is the model and it is severe in its simplicity: Moses puts words in his mouth, and he speaks them. Every prophet after him says the same thing in the same way — thus saith the LORD — and Paul describes the ministry as stewardship, where the one thing required in stewards is that a man be found faithful. A spokesman who improves on his message has not enriched it; he has stopped being a spokesman.

Aaron's later history supplies the warning that belongs with the office, and Scripture does not spare him. The man appointed to speak for Moses is the same man who, left alone at the foot of the mountain, made the golden calf and then explained it with one of the least convincing sentences in the canon: there came out this calf. Eloquence was his qualification and it did not preserve him. The gift of speech is a real gift and is no protection whatever against the fear of the people, which is what actually moved him. A church choosing men to speak for God should weigh Exodus 32 alongside Exodus 4.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dabar (H1696), to speak; peh (H6310), a mouth; nabiy (H5030), a prophet; elohim (H430), God.

expand to see more

Hebrew dabar (H1696) — to speak; the verb behind he shall be thy spokesman.

Hebrew peh (H6310) — a mouth; Aaron to be to Moses instead of a mouth.

Hebrew nabiy (H5030) — a prophet, a spokesman for God; Aaron so named at Exodus 7:1.

Hebrew elohim (H430) — God; Moses to Aaron instead of God, the source of the words.

Hebrew sum (H7760) — to put, to place; put words in his mouth.

Usage

"“he shall be thy spokesman unto the people” — the office defined."

"“put words in his mouth” — the message is not the speaker's own."

"“Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet” — the same relation restated."
